chapters.title: Market microstructure: from a chart to an actual trade
chapters.subtitle: The price you see and the price you can transact at are different questions.
chapters.takeaway: A trade requires available counterparties under specific order rules. Spread, depth, timing, and venue affect the outcome.

sections.title: Last price, bid, and ask describe different things
paragraphs: A candlestick summarizes completed trades. A quote describes displayed interest to transact under particular conditions. The bid is a price buyers are willing to pay; the ask is a price sellers are willing to accept. The highest displayed bid is the best bid and the lowest displayed ask is the best ask; the quoted spread is best ask minus best bid. FINRA links limited liquidity with greater difficulty transacting and wider spreads. The last completed trade can lie between current quotes or become stale after they move.

The main static book has best bid $49.90 for 300 shares and best ask $50.10 for 100 shares. The midpoint, the average of best bid and best ask, is ($49.90 + $50.10)/2 = $50; the spread is $0.20. Last trade is assumed $50, but that print does not supply a counterparty for a new order. A buyer seeking immediate execution consumes an available ask; an immediate seller consumes an available bid. The SEC notes that last-traded price need not equal the price obtained by a market order.

sections.title: The spread is a cost even before price moves
paragraphs: In a deliberately simplified example, buy 100 shares at $50.10 and immediately sell them at $49.90, with unchanged quotes, sufficient quantity, and no fees. The round trip loses $20. The midpoint never moved. This makes the spread visible as a trading friction that a backtest using only closing prices can omit. Real execution can differ through price improvement (execution at a better price than the current quote, possible but not guaranteed), partial fills, changing quotes, and other costs.

A twenty-cent spread has different proportional importance at different prices. Spread divided by midpoint gives a relative spread: $0.20/$50 = 0.4% in this example. That measure still omits size. A quote suitable for 100 shares may not support an order for 10,000 shares. When a trading method aims for small price changes or high turnover, even modest execution friction can materially alter its results. Test the cost model at the scale of the actual method.

sections.title: Walk a 250-share buy through the ladder
paragraphs: The figure lists displayed asks at $50.10 for 100 shares, $50.20 for 200, and $50.30 for 300. We assume these quantities remain fixed, no other accessible liquidity, and no competing orders arriving first. Those conditions deliberately create a small executable arithmetic model. They are not claims about a real order book’s stability.

A market buy order for 250 shares (a buy limit at $50.20 or higher would fill the same way here) first takes 100 at $50.10. It needs 150 more, which are taken from the 200 offered at $50.20. The third row is untouched. Fill value is 100 × 50.10 + 150 × 50.20 = $12,540. Divide by 250 to obtain the weighted fill price $50.16. The best ask $50.10 was available only for 100 shares; it was not a price offer for the whole order.

The ladder’s consumed/remaining columns make the sequence visible. The first ask is depleted, 50 remain at $50.20, and all 300 at $50.30 remain. Now compare a buy limit at $50.10 for the same 250 shares. It can execute immediately only against the 100 shares offered at $50.10. Under this static model it can take only 100 immediately; the other 150 remain unfilled under an ordinary resting instruction. If given an immediate-or-cancel instruction, that remainder is canceled.

A historical candle touching $50.10 does not establish either modeled outcome without the available quantities and timing. The static ladder is valuable precisely because it supplies those assumptions. Live quotes can change before the order arrives, accessible interest can exist elsewhere, and competing orders can consume it first. The SEC’s execution overview explains why order submission and execution are separate events.

tables.title: Two modeled fill instructions

sections.title: Different mechanisms can form opening and closing prices
paragraphs: An auction collects eligible buying and selling interest and applies exchange rules to determine a match. NYSE publishes opening and closing auction information, including indicative match prices and imbalance quantities. Those indications describe the state of the auction calculation, not a guarantee of the final auction price. Orders can change before the relevant deadlines, and exact procedures differ by venue and can change over time.

A large final volume bar can therefore include activity concentrated in a closing auction rather than the same style of continuous trading seen earlier in the day. That does not make the print unimportant. It does change what you can infer from it. If a strategy requires a closing transaction, study the actual auction mechanism and the time by which its order would have to exist. Knowing the final close afterward is not enough to assume participation at that price.

sections.title: Trading conditions vary across the session
paragraphs: The SEC’s extended-hours bulletin highlights lower liquidity, wider spreads, uncertain prices, and differences in available venues and order handling outside regular hours. A narrow daytime spread should not be assumed for an overnight news reaction. A quote from one view may also fail to represent the liquidity reachable through your broker at that moment. Broker routing is part of the transaction path, as Investor.gov’s execution overview explains.

For a fictional illustration, let the midpoint stay near $50 while the bid and ask separate from $49.99/$50.01 to $49.60/$50.40. A close-only chart could look motionless while an immediate round trip becomes much more expensive. This is why liquidity and volume are related but distinct. A daily share count describes accumulated activity; your execution depends on available interest when, where, and at what size you arrive.

sections.title: Measure costs against a named reference
paragraphs: Using decision-time midpoint $50 as reference, the main 250-share buy at average $50.16 is $0.16 per share above midpoint, or $40 total. Relative to the best ask $50.10, it is $0.06 higher on average, or $15. These are different benchmarks for the same fill; quoting slippage without identifying the reference leaves the comparison ambiguous.

Suppose the 300-share bid at $49.90 remains available after the modeled purchase and the position is immediately sold. Sale value is 250 × 49.90 = $12,475; purchase value $12,540; price-only round-trip loss is $65. On 250 shares the $0.20 spread alone costs $50; the remaining $15 is the extra $0.10 paid on the 150 shares taken at the second ask level. Per share the loss is $0.26, against $0.20 for the earlier 100-share round trip; that $0.06 difference is what reaching beyond the first quote cost.

A completed model record is now possible: “Decision reference midpoint $50; buy 250; static accessible asks 100@50.10 and at least 150@50.20; fills 100/150; mean $50.16; immediate sale assumption 250@49.90; loss $65 before fees.” If the bid changes or quantity disappears, that last result changes. Recording the assumptions makes the consequence inspectable.

For actual practice, record decision time, quote reference, order instruction, requested shares, individual fills, and unfilled remainder. A no-fee statement removes fees only; it does not remove spread or price movement. The planning and testing chapters use this distinction when translating a chart event into a cost-aware opportunity. You need enough mechanics to challenge impossible fills, without mastering every exchange rule.

example.title: Every fill has a quantity
example.text: The 250-share purchase consumes 100@$50.10 and 150@$50.20. Value $5,010+$7,530 = $12,540; weighted average $50.16. Unweighted mean $50.15 would give the two price levels equal influence despite unequal quantities. An immediate 250-share sale at the assumed unchanged $49.90 bid receives $12,475, producing a $65 price loss before fees.

Record 200 filled and 100 unfilled, not 300 filled at the limit. The supplied static availability is a modeling assumption; actual changing queues could produce a different execution.

glossary: The equal-weight arithmetic mean of the latest N observations; specify the price field and interval.
A recursive mean that assigns greater weight to newer observations; its seed and smoothing constant matter.
The delay caused when a summary retains earlier observations after current behavior changes.
Earlier observations used to initialize an indicator before its readings are treated as fully available.
A defined change in ordering between price and a reference, or between two references, across observations.
Percentage change from a selected earlier price: 100 × (current / earlier − 1).
A bounded oscillator comparing smoothed upward and downward changes within one instrument.
A fast EMA minus a slow EMA, commonly accompanied by a smoothed signal and a difference histogram.
A specified mismatch between selected price extremes and corresponding indicator readings; selection and recognition times must be stated.
The largest of high minus low and the absolute distances from the previous close to today’s high and low.
A smoothed measure of true-range magnitude, in price units, without directional information.
Envelopes around a moving average at a specified number of rolling price standard deviations.
Current activity divided by a specified historical baseline for a comparable interval.
Included prices averaged with share quantities as weights; bar-based calculations approximate transaction data.
A volume-weighted mean accumulated from an explicitly selected starting observation.
Cumulative volume added for higher closes, subtracted for lower closes, and unchanged for equal closes.
A movement giving back a specified fraction of a selected earlier move.
One instrument’s value divided by a comparator’s value to describe proportional relative performance.
A cumulative sum of advancing-issue count minus declining-issue count in a defined universe.
Participation measured across an explicitly defined population rather than solely through an aggregate index.
An interval whose final eligible closing observation exists under the chosen boundaries; a developing bar remains provisional.
A discontinuity between defined sampled prices, often a session open versus the prior session close.
The difference between the quoted ask and bid; it does not alone describe available quantity.
Quantities offered at successive prices in the observed market view, subject to change and coverage limits.
Execution difference from a specified reference price; the reference must be named.
Alias: see Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP).
A histogram grouping included trading volume by declared price bins and observation period.
The highest-volume row in the specified volume profile; it is a historical concentration, not an open order.
An instruction to execute immediately and cancel any unfilled remainder, subject to broker availability.

tasks.title: Read an unfamiliar price path
tasks.question: Use fictional closes 40, 42, 41, 43, 44, 46, 45, 44, 43, 42, 43, 44. Compute three-session SMA at sessions 10 and 11 and three-session ROC at 11. Under the chapter’s close-based crossover rule, classify session 11. Explain why its ROC sign need not match its SMA position.
solution: At 10, SMA = (44+43+42)/3 = $43. At 11, SMA = (43+42+43)/3 = $42.6667. Session 10 close $42 is below its mean; session 11 close $43 exceeds its mean, so an up-cross is known after 11 closes.

Three-session ROC at 11 compares session 8 close $44: 100 × (43/44−1) = −2.2727%. Price can be above a recent mean while below a selected earlier close. These are different questions, not contradictory facts.

tasks.title: Match the tool to the evidence
tasks.question: For that close-only path, which of SMA, ROC, RSI, ATR, exact transaction VWAP, and exact volume-by-price profile can be computed from the supplied information? Then check the volume-tools chapter’s 12-trade tape by reconciling VWAP and profile totals.
solution: SMA and ROC are computable with declared lookbacks. RSI is computable once gain/loss smoothing, seed, lookback, and flat-case convention are fixed. ATR needs highs/lows and previous closes, which are absent; transaction VWAP and exact profile need prices and quantities of included trades, which are absent from this close-only path.
